newsitem.title: FRANCE: French govt not to act on French car job cut plea.
newsitem.headline: French govt not to act on French car job cut plea.

text.p: The French government has decided not to act on a request that it back a five-year early retirement plan proposed by carmakers Renault and PSA Peugeot Citroen, an industry ministry source said on Wednesday.
"The government considered the case and decided today not to commit itself by way of exemptions and on a multiannual basis," the source said in response to a query.

Renault and Peugeot had been seeking government help with funding of plans for costly early retirements which industry sources say would have been to the tune of 40,000 for the two companies in total.

While neither company has ever officially confirmed precise figures, Peugeot chairman Jacques Calvet has said he wanted the government to foot a bigger share of the bill to finance early retirements help the industry slim and rejuvenate its workforce to increase its competitiveness.
Calvet has also warned that he could be forced to resort to layoffs if government approval for the proposals was not forthcoming.

The industry ministry source said the government, which commissioned a report on the car industry and received it in January, had decided not to give the green light to the plans as presented by the two companies.
The government recognised that, generally speaking, the car sector was highly competitive and that productivity gains would have to be found, said the source.

"But one of the answers given is that the labour aspect, the labour dimension, cannot provide the solution on its own to the search for productivity gains," said the source, adding that the government would be open to more general talks with the industry players on the problem.
Renault declined to comment and a Peugeot spokesman said the matter had not been one of a very precise demand, but rather one of registering the scale of the problem.

He said Peugeot was "not surprised by the government's decision given the difficult labour climate at present" and that the pace of scaling down staff should continue at the pace set between 1985 and 1995, reductions in the region of two to three percent per year.
